item.title: Nix Sandbox Provides Declarative Security for AI CLI Agents
item.description:
Nix Sandbox Provides Declarative Security for AI CLI Agents

A new lightweight, declarative sandboxing tool has been introduced for AI agents operating on Linux and macOS. Built using Nix, the project aims to prevent “YOLO mode” agents from performing destructive actions such as deleting home directories, force pushing to main branches, or publishing SSH keys online.

🧩 How it works

The sandbox supports any CLI-based AI agent and utilizes underlying system tools to create restricted environments:

  • Linux: Uses bubblewrap.
  • macOS: Uses sandbox-exec.

Access controls are defined declaratively, allowing developers to specify exactly what the agent can read, write, or execute. By default, network access is open, but it can be filtered to specific domains. Ports are closed by default unless explicitly exposed or connected to.

⚙️ Key details

The sandbox enforces strict boundaries on file system access and environment variables. Only changes to the project directory and declared read/write paths are persisted; all other writes, including to the agent’s home directory, are discarded upon exit.

Category Behavior
Project Directory Read/write access to the launch directory or a fixed workspaceDir.
Declared State Read/write access via rwDirs/rwFiles; read-only access via roDirs/roFiles.
Allowed Packages Binaries listed in allowedPackages are added to the PATH, alongside bash and cacert.
Environment Restricted to declared environment variables only.
Git Supports git commands, including those launched within a worktree.
Nix Disabled by default, though agents can be explicitly permitted to run nix commands.

🚀 Availability

The repository provides templates for common agent CLIs. To get started, users can use a flake template which creates a flake.nix in the project directory. For those not using flakes, a plain shell.nix setup is available. Users can adapt existing templates or contribute new ones by adjusting parameters such as pkg, binName, outName, allowedDomains, and required rwDirs for configuration and cache.

#Nix #AIagents #Linux #macOS #Sandboxing #DevOps

Source: archie-judd/agent-sandbox.nix

item.title: pCloud Pass users report unauthorized device connections following cyberattack
item.description:
pCloud Pass users report unauthorized device connections following cyberattack

The pCloud Pass password manager was recently targeted by a cyberattack, resulting in users reporting that unknown devices had connected to their accounts, some with two-factor authentication (2FA) enabled. The attack was contained by the pCloud team, though a small number of user email addresses were exposed.

🔍 Overview

According to pCloud, a cyberattack targeting pCloud Pass occurred and was promptly contained. The company stated that a small number of pCloud Pass user email addresses were exposed and that login attempts were made. The system automatically sent notifications to each of these affected addresses.

⚙️ Key details

  • Users reported receiving notifications warning that an unfamiliar device named “pd” connected to their account from IP address 45.131.244.7 in Luxembourg.
  • The IP address is reportedly part of pCloud’s own infrastructure.
  • Notifications were received by customers who had 2FA enabled.
  • Some users who never used the password manager, including those with deleted storage accounts, also received the alerts.
  • PCloud stated the attack was isolated to the password manager, and cloud storage services were not affected.
  • Passwords, notes, and other information stored in pCloud Pass are encrypted on customer devices and were not compromised.
  • It is unknown whether encrypted password vaults were accessed or stolen during the attack.
  • A reader noted that the “Open settings” link in the email notifications pointed to passqa1.pcloud.com, a QA environment, rather than the production site.

💡 Why it matters

Threat actors who obtain encrypted password vaults can attempt to crack them offline, bypassing the service’s login rate limits and two-factor authentication protections. This risk was demonstrated in the 2022 LastPass breach, where stolen encrypted password vaults were linked to cryptocurrency thefts after attackers cracked weak or reused master passwords.

🛡️ Security advice

  • pCloud is warning customers to watch for phishing attacks.
  • The company states it will never ask for master passwords or recovery words over email, phone, or chat.
  • PCloud noted that advancements in artificial intelligence are accelerating the discovery of software vulnerabilities, though it did not state that this specific attack was AI-powered.

#pCloud #PasswordManager #Cybersecurity #DataBreach #2FA

Source: pCloud confirms password manager hack after suspicious login alerts

item.title: Q-Dir and DesktopOK Installers Compromised with Python-Based Malware
item.description:
Q-Dir and DesktopOK Installers Compromised with Python-Based Malware

Official distribution channels for the popular Windows utilities Q-Dir and DesktopOK were compromised to deliver trojanized installers containing Python-based remote access malware, according to a report from AhnLab’s Security Intelligence Center (ASEC).

🧩 Malware Capabilities

The malicious installers fetch a Python Remote Access Trojan (RAT) that registers a scheduled task to persist on infected devices. The malware supports the following capabilities:

  • Shell command and Python code execution
  • File transfer
  • Screenshot capture
  • System information collection, including a list of active security products

📊 Impacted Versions

ASEC confirmed that the compromise affected both new downloads and updates for existing installations. Not all listed versions were infected. The following release versions are impacted:

Product Affected Versions
Q-Dir 12.83.0.0, 12.84.0.0, 12.85.0.0
DesktopOK 12.82.0.0, 12.85.0.0

🕵️ Security Detection Evasion

The malware collects a list of 1,206 processes matching various antivirus and endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools to relay to the command and control server. This allows operators to plan their next actions without getting detected. The targeted security products include:

  • AhnLab V3
  • CrowdStrike Falcon
  • SentinelOne
  • rend Micro
  • Avast
  • McAfee
  • ESET
  • Symantec
  • Kaspersky
  • Bitdefender
  • Sophos
  • Fortinet
  • Elastic Security
  • Malwarebytes
  • FireEye

🛡️ Remediation and Verification

AhnLab researchers provided SHA-256 hashes to help users distinguish legitimate installers from malicious ones. Users are advised to check their downloads against the SHA-256 published on the official download page.

Removing a trojanized version of Q-Dir or DesktopOK does not ensure the elimination of the Python RAT. Users who recently installed or updated these tools should treat their system as potentially compromised and check for:

  • Suspicious Python execution environments
  • Scheduled tasks
  • Traces of external network communication

The trojanized versions are digitally signed using a certificate issued to the legitimate developer, Nenad Hrg, who distributes the tools through the SoftwareOK website. ASEC could not determine how the installers were replaced or the timeframe during which the malicious versions were distributed.

#WindowsSecurity #SupplyChainAttack #Trojan #QDir #DesktopOK #Cybersecurity

Source: Q-Dir and DesktopOK Windows utilities compromised to push Python RAT

item.title: 12-Year-Old Linux NFS Vulnerability Lets Remote Attackers Gain Root
item.description:
12-Year-Old Linux NFS Vulnerability Lets Remote Attackers Gain Root

A 12‑year‑old critical vulnerability in the Linux kernel’s NFS server, CVE‑2026‑99362, lets remote attackers gain root privileges.

🔍 Overview

  • The flaw, dubbed NFS2ROOT by OpenSec, is a heap buffer overflow in the nfsd server.
  • Remote attackers can send crafted requests that write beyond an allocated buffer.
  • Successful exploitation corrupts kernel memory and grants root access on exposed Linux servers.

🧩 How it Works

  • An attacker sends malicious NFSv4.1 requests causing the server to write past a buffer.
  • This allows reading of kernel memory, bypassing KASLR.
  • A callback is placed in a released memory area that executes a command.
  • When the connection closes, the kernel runs the embedded command with root privileges.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Vulnerability exists since Linux kernel 3.16 (March 2014).
  • Affects kernels older than 6.12.117, 6.18.61, 7.3.2, or 7.4‑rc1 when nfsd (v4.1 or 4.2) is loaded and TCP port 2049 is reachable over the Internet.
  • No user interaction required; low‑complexity attack.

🚀 Availability

  • ANSSI’s Jérémy Jean submitted a fix in August; the patch was shared with NFSD maintainers in late September.

💡 Why it Matters

  • No wild exploitation reports yet, but the flaw can give attackers full control.
  • Apply the latest kernel security updates immediately and reboot.
  • If patching isn’t possible, restrict TCP port 2049 to trusted clients or disable nfs-server in /etc/nfs.conf.
  • Kernel hardening does not remove the overflow; patch every host.
  • Monitor for signs such as kernel warnings from nfsd4_check_resp_size, shells spawned by kernel workers, bursts of short NFSv4.1 sessions, and kernel oopses with nfsd4_* or svc_* frames.

📚 Related Flaws

  • Other privilege escalation bugs disclosed this year include RefluXFS, CIFSwitch, Dirty Frag, Fragnesia, PinTheft, Copy Fail, Pack2TheRoot, and DirtyDecrypt/DirtyCBC.

#Linux #NFS #KernelSecurity #CVE202699362 #PrivilegeEscalation #CyberSecurity

Source: New NFS2ROOT Linux flaw can let attackers gain root privileges

item.title: Gondolin introduces secure, isolated micro-VMs for AI agents running generated code
item.description:
Gondolin introduces secure, isolated micro-VMs for AI agents running generated code

Gondolin is a new agent sandbox that runs AI-generated code inside local Linux micro-VMs, providing programmable network and filesystem control. It addresses security risks from autonomous code execution by isolating agents while maintaining controlled access to network resources and credentials.

🧩 How it works

The system uses a TypeScript Control Plane with Linux microvm setup. Generated code is executed inside a fast local Linux micro-VM (using libkrun when available, with QEMU fallback) that keeps network and filesystem access under host-side policy control.

🔍 Architecture

A key security feature is that the guest VM only sees placeholder tokens, while the real secret is injected by the host only for allowed destinations, including Authorization: Basic ... flows.

⚙️ Key details

Platform Support

  • Node.js 22.19 or newer required
  • npm install @earendil-works/gondolin installs the Gondolin daemon (gondolind) and platform packages
  • Works on macOS and Linux on arm64 and x64

Execution Backend

  • Uses libkrun on Apple silicon and Linux x86_64 with read/write /dev/kvm
  • Falls back to QEMU on other hosts or when qemu backend is selected

Policy Control

  • Programmable HTTP/TLS egress policy with allowlists and request/response hooks
  • Daemon-side policies via self-contained JavaScript (createDjsHooks(), --hooks-script)
  • Configurable DNS behavior, rootfs modes, and runtime sizing

Session Management

Useful session commands include:

  • List running sessions
  • Attach to an existing session
  • Snapshot a running session (stops it)
  • Resume from snapshot id/path

Guest Images and Storage

  • Default guest image: alpine-base:latest (downloaded from built-in registry on first use)
  • Images cached locally (~200MB+)
  • Disk checkpoints (snapshots) with resume support
  • Custom image builds via Alpine-based pipeline with optional OCI rootfs source

File System and Network Features

  • Programmable VFS mounts allowing custom file system behavior in JavaScript
  • Ingress gateway to expose guest HTTP services on host (--listen, vm.enableIngress())
  • SSH support: host -> guest access (vm.enableSsh()) and optional guest -> upstream allowlisted SSH egress (proxied, exec-oriented)

Daemon Architecture

The VM runs under a static Rust daemon (gondolind) that can operate on another machine without Node.js, while policy, hooks, and credentials remain local.

#AIagents #Security #Virtualization #MicroVM #TypeScript #Rust

Source: earendil-works/gondolin

item.title: Amazon Cognito SLA Enhanced to 99.99 Percent for Plus Plan Starting November 2026
item.description:
Amazon Cognito SLA Enhanced to 99.99 Percent for Plus Plan Starting November 2026

Amazon Cognito’s Service Level Agreement (SLA) for user pools on the Plus feature plan is increasing from 99.9 percent to 99.99 percent, effective November 1, 2026. This enhancement ensures tighter uptime guarantees for applications that rely on Cognito’s sign-in and access management capabilities.

📌 Why It Matters

Sign-in is the front door to your application. If your customer identity and access management (CIAM) layer is unavailable, users can’t sign in or refresh their sessions, preventing access to the rest of your application. The application’s availability directly depends on the availability of your identity layer.

Many customers use Amazon Cognito for applications with strict availability requirements, such as patient portals and retail checkout flows. They need the services they build on to support high availability. The 99.99 percent SLA provides 10 times better reliability than the previous 99.9 percent commitment.

⚙️ Key Details

The SLA improvement applies specifically to user pools on the Plus feature plan. User pools on Essentials and Lite feature plans will continue with the 99.9 percent Service Commitment.

  • 99.99 Percent SLA (Plus plan): Reduces allowable monthly downtime from ~43 minutes to ~4.3 minutes in a 30-day month.
  • 99.9 Percent SLA (Essentials and Lite plans): Remains unchanged.
  • Existing Plus plan user pools automatically receive the new commitment; no action is required.

The SLA measures availability per AWS Region, calculating the Monthly Uptime Percentage based on 5-minute intervals and excluding HTTP 500 or 503 errors. Intervals with no requests count as 100 percent available.

🚀 Availability Performance

Historical data shows strong performance relative to these commitments.

  • Availability was at or above 99.99 percent in 10 of the 12 months.
  • It was below 99.99 percent in January (99.988 percent) and March (99.979 percent), but stayed above the previous 99.9 percent commitment in both months and reached 99.99 percent the following month.

🛠️ Switching to Plus

Organizations can switch user pools to the Plus feature plan to qualify for the improved SLA.

This can be done via:

  • AWS Management Console: Navigate to User Pools, select your pool, go to Settings > Feature Plans tab, and choose “Switch to Plus.”
  • AWS CLI: Using the Update-user-pool command or UpdateUserPool API operation. Note that unspecified parameters reset to default values.

Before switching, users should compare features and costs in the user pool feature plans and Amazon Cognito pricing documentation.

#AWS #Cognito #SLA #IAM #HighAvailability #UserPools

Source: Planning for 99.99 percent availability with the Amazon Cognito Plus feature plan | Amazon Web Services

item.title: AWS Launches AWS-LC, a Standardized Cryptographic Library for PQC
item.description:
AWS Launches AWS-LC, a Standardized Cryptographic Library for PQC

AWS has released AWS‑LC, a unified cryptographic library that supports post‑quantum algorithms while maintaining compatibility, assurance, and performance.

🔍 Overview

  • AWS‑LC is a general‑purpose cryptographic library maintained by AWS.
  • Derived from BoringSSL, which originated from OpenSSL.
  • It provides hybrid post‑quantum key exchange via s2n‑tls for service endpoints.
  • It underlies aws‑lc‑rs (Rust), rustls, and the Amazon Corretto Crypto Provider (Java).
  • AWS‑LC keeps an OpenSSL‑compatible API so applications can replace algorithms without rewriting.
  • AWS uses it across its services; if you’ve called an AWS API, AWS‑LC was used on the server side.

🧩 How it Works

  • AWS‑LC uses formal verification to prove selected algorithm implementations correct.
  • It optimizes algorithm implementations to reduce latency and compute costs of new algorithms.
  • For TLS, AWS‑LC libssl keeps an OpenSSL‑compatible API; most applications that use OpenSSL for TLS build against it with small changes.
  • Applications that call libcrypto directly may need more work, as the API differs in places.
  • When new algorithms are added, s2n‑tls, s2n‑quic, aws‑lc‑rs, and the Amazon Corretto Crypto Provider adopt them automatically.
  • Hybrid ML‑KEM key exchange is enabled through existing TLS configuration APIs.
  • 1Password used AWS‑LC to move clients to hybrid post‑quantum key exchange with only a one‑line Cargo.toml change and no application code changes.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Three properties that reduce cost and friction of cryptographic updates:
    • Compatibility: update doesn’t require application changes.
    • Assurance: new code can be trusted when it ships.
    • Performance: new algorithm doesn’t add much computational overhead or latency.
  • AWS‑LC long‑term support (LTS) releases keep a stable application binary interface (ABI).
  • Applications link once, then take library updates without a rebuild.
  • One update reaches every application on the host when each process restarts.

🚀 Availability

  • AWS‑LC is available as an AWS‑LC library for C/C++.
  • The Rust bindings are available via aws‑lc‑rs.
  • Java integration is available via Amazon Corretto Crypto Provider.

💡 Why It Matters

  • Every cryptographic algorithm has an expiration date; traditional ones like MD5 and SHA‑1 have been retired.
  • Standards are revised and flaws found in implementations.
  • PQC is accelerating the pace of adding new algorithms and removing old ones to keep up with regulations and risk.
  • The move to PQC has government and regulator deadlines; PQC will progress in phases to enable hybrid and pure post‑quantum algorithms.
  • Each change reaches systems as a software library update; the practical question is how often you can roll out a new version and its cost.
  • By standardizing on a single library like AWS‑LC, organizations reduce ongoing responsibility and operational risk.

📊 Performance Impact

  • TLS1.3 setup time on Graviton4 is measured for different algorithms; the figure shows impact of new algorithms.

  • Client‑server architecture using hybrid ML‑KEM.

#Cryptography #PostQuantum #AWSLC #Security

Source: Make post-quantum cryptography updates routine with AWS-LC | Amazon Web Services

item.title: AWS Sign-In Adds Enterprise-Managed Authorization for AI Agents via ID-JAG
item.description:
AWS Sign-In Adds Enterprise-Managed Authorization for AI Agents via ID-JAG

AWS Sign‑In is adding Enterprise‑Managed Authorization (EMA) that lets organizations authorize AI agents such as Claude to access AWS MCP Server using existing enterprise identity providers like Okta.

🔍 Overview

  • EMA extends the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to let enterprises centrally control AI‑application access to protected resources.
  • It uses the Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID‑JAG), an OAuth‑based grant that works with enterprise IdPs.

🧩 How it works

  1. Employee authentication – The employee signs in to an AI application (e.g., Claude) through single sign‑on (SSO) with an enterprise IdP such as Okta.
  2. ID‑JAG request – When the AI application needs to call an AWS MCP Server, it asks the IdP for an ID‑JAG assertion for the target resource.
  3. Enterprise authorization – The IdP evaluates policies defined by administrators and, if authorized, issues a short‑lived, signed ID‑JAG assertion.
  4. Token exchange with AWS Sign‑In – The AI application sends the ID‑JAG to the AWS Sign‑In OAuth token endpoint. AWS validates the assertion, checks the associated IAM role trust policy via AWS STS, and issues an OAuth access token linked to that role.
  5. Access AWS MCP Server – The AI application presents the OAuth token to the AWS MCP Server. The server validates the token, and the IAM role’s policies determine which AWS operations the agent may perform.

⚙️ Key details

  • No extra credentials – Employees do not need to manage long‑term AWS credentials or complete separate consent flows.
  • Policy‑driven – Administrators define access rules in the IdP, eliminating per‑user authorizations for each MCP server.
  • IAM enforcement – After token issuance, standard IAM role permissions control the actions the AI agent can perform on AWS resources.
  • Short‑lived assertions – ID‑JAG tokens are short‑lived and signed, limiting exposure if compromised.

🛠️ Prerequisites

  • An AWS account with permission to configure IAM identity providers, roles, and policies.
  • An Okta organization with administrative rights to manage applications and Cross‑App Access policies.
  • An AI application (e.g., Claude) that supports EMA and ID‑JAG.
  • Access to an AWS MCP Server that supports OAuth‑based Enterprise‑Managed Authorization.
  • The AWS Region where the integration will be configured.

#AWS #AIAgents #EnterpriseAuthorization #Okta #OAuth

Source: Secure agentic access to AWS with Enterprise-Managed Authorization | Amazon Web Services

item.title: AWS Completes Second ISO/IEC 42001 Surveillance Audit for AI Services
item.description:
AWS Completes Second ISO/IEC 42001 Surveillance Audit for AI Services

AWS successfully completed its second surveillance audit for ISO/IEC 42001:2023, the standard for Artificial Intelligence Management Systems (AIMS). This audit resulted in no findings and marks the addition of a new service to the certification program.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Audit Timeline: In November 2024, AWS was the first major cloud service provider to announce the ISO/IEC 42001 accredited certification for AI services. The second surveillance audit was completed in November 2026.
  • Audit Result: The audit concluded with no findings.
  • New Coverage: AWS DevOps Agent has been added as a new service covered under the ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification program.

📄 Services Under ISO/IEC 42001

The following services are covered under the AWS ISO/IEC 42001:2023 certification program:

Service Status
Amazon Bedrock Originally certified in November 2024
Amazon Q Business Originally certified in November 2024
Amazon Textract Originally certified in November 2024
Amazon Transcribe Originally certified in November 2024
AWS DevOps Agent Added during the second surveillance audit in November 2026

💡 Why It Matters

This completion demonstrates the continuous commitment by AWS to responsible AI practices. With this independent validation, customers gain assurance regarding the commitment to responsible AI, which enables them to build and operate AI applications responsibly using AWS services.

🚀 Accessing Certifications

  • A full list of AWS services certified under ISO and CSA STAR is available on the AWS ISO and CSA STAR Certified page.
  • Customers can also access these certifications through the AWS Management Console for AWS Artifact.

item.title: AWS Enhances API and AI Endpoint Security
item.description:
AWS Enhances API and AI Endpoint Security

AWS has launched new capabilities to discover and protect APIs and AI endpoints, addressing the evolving landscape of digital business and AI agent interactions.

🔍 Overview

  • AWS has introduced new features to help discover and protect APIs and AI endpoints.
  • This includes API Portal in Amazon API Gateway, API Security, and AI Security managed rule groups in AWS WAF.

🧩 How it works

  • API Portal discovers APIs and AI endpoints from configuration and live traffic.
  • API Security protects against broken object level authorization, authentication attacks, and reconnaissance.
  • AI Security identifies AI traffic, validates requests, and checks prompts and responses through Amazon Bedrock Guardrails.

⚙️ Key details

  • API Portal is available in the Amazon API Gateway console.
  • API Security and AI Security are available in the AWS WAF console.
  • The new features work with Amazon CloudFront, Amazon API Gateway REST APIs, and Application Load Balancer.

🚀 Availability

  • API Portal, API Security, and AI Security are generally available today.

💡 Why it matters

  • APIs have run digital businesses for over a decade.
  • In 2026, AI endpoints joined them, leading to a need for new security measures.
  • AI agents now act on behalf of users, requiring robust protection of APIs and AI endpoints.

item.title: NVIDIA's OpenShell runtime adds policy enforcement for autonomous AI agents
item.description:
NVIDIA’s OpenShell runtime adds policy enforcement for autonomous AI agents

NVIDIA has contributed OpenShell, an open source runtime for autonomous AI agents, to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation (CNCF), where it is now a Sandbox project. The Apache 2.0 licensed tool focuses on enforcing security policies across agent interactions, ensuring that agents only access resources explicitly permitted by predefined rules.

🔍 Overview

OpenShell acts as a runtime layer that monitors and restricts the behavior of autonomous AI agents. It enforces declared policies on every file access, system call, and network connection. A key feature of the runtime is its ability to verify which specific binary initiates a network connection, preventing agents from exploiting trusted applications to send data to unauthorized destinations.

🧩 How it works

The enforcement mechanism operates at multiple levels of the stack:

  • Network Policy: Rules can specify that only certain binaries may reach specific endpoints. For example, a policy can restrict the Snyk binary to only access api.snyk.io, preventing the agent from using Snyk’s access to exfiltrate data elsewhere.
  • Credential Handling: OpenShell holds API keys and injects them only into requests bound for approved endpoints. In a test build involving Claude Code, Anthropic keys never entered the sandbox environment.
  • Default Denial: New sandboxes start with no network access. When an agent attempts to reach a new host, OpenShell blocks the request and generates a draft rule for human approval.
  • MCP Server Governance: Enforcement runs through the agent’s hooks at tool-call time. This covers local Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers that do not touch the network. If an agent calls a tool on an unapproved server, the governance system stops the call and identifies the responsible policy.

⚙️ Key details

A reference build combines OpenShell with specific security controls to demonstrate the architecture:

Component Function
Base Image NVIDIA’s own Ubuntu base image
Integrated Tools Claude Code and four Snyk controls
Startup Scanning Agent supply chain security scans the sandbox, flagging potential prompt injection and insecure credential handling with specific line numbers
Code Security Snyk Studio’s “Secure at Inception” hook scans agent output, flagging issues like SQL injection and holding the turn until fixes are applied
Inventory Each sandbox appears in Evo as a distinct machine alongside developer laptops and Docker Sandboxes

The architecture relies on binaries being fixed at build time and checksum-verified. Because OpenShell only permits program execution from system folders such as /usr, tools like Snyk are built directly into the image rather than installed at runtime.

🚀 Availability

OpenShell is available as an open source project under the Apache 2.0 license. The tested version was OpenShell 0.1.6. A single run.sh command can build the reference image, store credentials in OpenShell, and start the sandbox with a pre-approved network policy.

#NVIDIA #OpenShell #AIAgents #Security #CNCF

Source: How to Secure AI Coding Agents in NVIDIA OpenShell with Evo | Snyk

item.title: OpenRouter Removes Three AI Providers After Data‑Handling Violations
item.description:
OpenRouter Removes Three AI Providers After Data‑Handling Violations

OpenRouter removed three AI providers from its platform after discovering they had violated data‑handling policies and exposed sensitive data.

🔍 Overview

  • OpenRouter revoked Zero Data Retention (ZDR) eligibility for 125 endpoints as a precaution.
  • The company notified all potentially affected customers.
  • OpenRouter removed the leaking inference providers: Together AI, Phala, and Novita.
  • Atlas Cloud voluntarily withdrew its models from OpenRouter pending security testing.

🧩 How it Works

  • OpenRouter is an AI model broker that lets developers access models from different companies using a single API key.
  • When an app sends a request, OpenRouter forwards it to the provider that runs the selected model and passes the answer back.

⚙️ Key Details

  • Dragos alerted OpenRouter after sending two million test prompts containing unique tracking links or decoy credentials.
  • Dragos detected activity indicating data from at least three AI providers was exposed.
  • Dragos found that in some cases credentials were leaked to outsiders and used in the wild.
  • Dragos said: “We observed activity indicating that data from at least three AI providers was exposed. Our seeded test prompts were used in attempts to access our controlled test systems and canary AWS accounts.”
  • OpenRouter said there was no breach on its own systems, pointing the leak to the provider level.
  • The providers’ incidents and responses:
Provider Incident Response
Together AI Exposed a GitHub repository credential, allowing unauthorized download of prompt samples (June–July) involving MiniMax M3, GLM‑5.2, Kimi K2.6 Tightening security controls; strengthening zero‑data retention; advising users to rotate secrets
Phala Server processing DeepSeek V4 Flash 0731 requests compromised; credentials obtained from affected VMs (Oct 21‑22, possibly up to Nov 8) Tightening security controls; strengthening zero‑data retention; advising users to rotate secrets
Novita Routing misconfiguration forwarded MiniMax requests to MiniMax’s official API (May 28‑Nov 11) Tightening security controls; strengthening zero‑data retention; advising users to rotate secrets
Atlas Cloud Voluntarily withdrew models pending security testing after a third‑party incident —
  • All four providers are tightening security controls, strengthening their zero‑data retention or data deletion policies, and advising potentially impacted users to rotate any secrets that may have been exposed.
  • OpenRouter is adapting Dragos’ tests for ongoing use to check whether AI providers forward or leak user requests/responses to third parties.
  • OpenRouter will require validation before restoring ZDR eligibility.

💡 Why it Matters

  • The leaks exposed sensitive data and credentials to unauthorized parties, highlighting the importance of strict data‑handling policies for AI model brokers.
  • OpenRouter’s response—removing the offending providers, revoking ZDR eligibility, and adopting continuous testing—illustrates how platform operators can mitigate risks when provider security is compromised.

#OpenRouter #AI #DataSecurity #ModelBroker #ZeroDataRetention

Source: OpenRouter drops AI providers over leaked prompts and secrets

item.title: OpenHack v2.0.0 adds local AI security scanning to your source code
item.description:
OpenHack v2.0.0 adds local AI security scanning to your source code

OpenHack, a local AI security scanner for source code, has released version 2.0.0, introducing a new harness that maps codebases and assigns focused source reviews.

🔍 Overview

OpenHack is a local AI security scanner designed for source code. The v2 harness maps your codebase, assigns focused source reviews, challenges candidate findings, and judges the evidence. All scan history, findings, notes, and configuration remain in your local workspace.

🧩 How it works

The standalone executable includes the Bun runtime and dashboard assets, meaning no separate Bun, Node.js, Python, or package installation is required to run it. An AI provider is required to perform a scan, and API-key mode functions without additional provider software. OpenHack retains control of the scanning workflow and source tools. Subscription adapters invoke the provider CLI in an isolated temporary directory with its native execution tools disabled, reusing the CLI’s authentication without copying login tokens.

⚙️ Key details

item.title: Windows hotpatch update causes ERROR_ALLOTTED_SPACE_EXCEEDED error
item.description:
Windows hotpatch update causes ERROR_ALLOTTED_SPACE_EXCEEDED error

Devices that installed the November 2026 hotpatch update may experience errors when installing, launching, or running some applications. The error displayed is similar to “ERROR_ALLOTTED_SPACE_EXCEEDED (0xC0000099)”.

🧩 How it works

Current investigation suggests this issue occurs for applications that load the 32-bit Windows Installer DLL, found as msi.dll. This can happen more frequently with 32-bit applications, but can also occur for 64-bit applications under certain conditions.

⚙️ Key details

  • Affected Systems: This known issue impacts systems that have installed the hotpatch updates pushed through Windows Autopatch. It should not impact systems that have installed the standard November 2026 Patch Tuesday security updates.
  • Workaround: Users must edit the Windows Registry to increase the HotPatchTableSize.
  • Registry Procedure:
    1. Open the Windows Registry by typing “regedit” in the Start menu and selecting Registry Editor.
    2. Navigate to the HKLM\SYSTEM\CurrentControlSet\Control\Session Manager\Memory Management folder.
    3. Locate the “HotPatchTableSize” registry key, open it, and set the Value to “2000”.
    4. Close the registry editor and restart the device.
  • Warning: Microsoft advised backing up the registry and ensuring knowledge of how to restore it before modifying it.

🚀 Availability

  • Windows Autopatch History: Microsoft first announced Windows Autopatch in April 2022, stating it would be available for free to customers with a Windows 10/11 Enterprise E3 license or greater starting in July 2022.
  • Public Preview: The feature reached public preview in early June and has been generally available since July 2022.
  • Default Policy: Microsoft stated in March that it would turn on hotpatch security updates by default for all eligible Windows devices managed through the Microsoft Graph API and Microsoft Intune, after the May 2026 Windows security updates are installed.
  • Recent Fix: One month after the March announcement, Microsoft fixed a Windows Autopatch bug that caused driver updates restricted by administrative policies to deploy on some Autopatch-managed Windows devices belonging to customers in the European Union.

item.title: Configuring OAuth for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity and Snowflake MCP Servers
item.description:
Configuring OAuth for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity and Snowflake MCP Servers

Enterprises extending authentication and authorization controls into the agentic layer often require broad service account permissions or custom-built auth integrations that add operational overhead. When an AI agent running on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore needs to call the Snowflake-managed MCP server through the Model Context Protocol, enterprises must determine how the agent authenticates.

🔍 Overview

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway connects AI agents to external tool providers through MCP server targets, targeting the Snowflake-managed MCP server which surfaces Cortex Search and Cortex Analyst as MCP tools. The Gateway aggregates capabilities of its configured targets into a single unified catalog presented to the agent as one tools/list response. The core focus is outbound authentication for Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, detailing how it obtains and presents OAuth tokens to the Snowflake-managed MCP server.

⚙️ Key details

  • Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity acts as the credential broker, where the Gateway obtains a workload token by calling GetWorkloadAccessTokenForJWT, then calls GetResourceOauth2Token against the configured provider.
  • AgentCore Identity owns the token vault, token refresh, and user-to-token binding, automatically fetching, caching, and refreshing tokens.
  • AgentCore Identity supports three OAuth configurations spanning two grant types (authorization_code and client_credentials).
  • Snowflake OAuth allows Snowflake to act as its own OAuth authorization server with each user authenticating directly through the Authorization Code grant (3LO) without an external IdP.
  • Three-legged OAuth uses a third-party Identity Provider where users authenticate through corporate SSO with the Authorization Code grant, and Snowflake trusts IdP-issued JWTs through its External OAuth security integration.
  • Two-legged OAuth pattern uses a third-party IdP with a shared service user authenticating through the client_credentials grant, requiring no user interaction or consent, making it ideal for machine-to-machine workloads.
  • AgentCore Identity also supports an on-behalf-of (OBO) grant (TOKEN_EXCHANGE) that delivers per-user identity for unattended workloads without a consent prompt.
  • An API-key credential provider supports Snowflake Programmatic Access Tokens, though OAuth is focused on for per-user attribution and automatic token refresh.

item.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore adds EKS‑run agent with Okta‑driven governance
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore adds EKS‑run agent with Okta‑driven governance

A second coding agent was added on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) and wired through the same Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway. The update shows that the gateway‑based front door works regardless of where an agent runs, while keeping the Okta‑driven delegation and Cedar policy enforcement intact.

🔍 Overview

  • The original agent runs on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime and is invoked for signed‑in users through Okta Cross App Access (XAA).
  • Okta decides which agent may act for a user and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Identity redeems Okta’s grant inside the agent.
  • The new addition is a second agent (agent B) deployed on Amazon EKS, using its own Okta identity but following the identical request flow.

🏗️ Architecture

  • All agents reach a single Gateway endpoint; the Gateway holds the target registry and redeems the Okta grant.
  • The topology consists of:
    • 1 agent (original) + 1 agent (EKS)
    • 2 Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers acting as Gateway targets
    • Authorization checks embedded in each MCP server
  • Request flow (illustrated for agent A):
    1. User signs in; the backend‑for‑frontend (BFF) exchanges the ID token for an Identity Assertion JWT Authorization Grant (ID‑JAG).
    2. BFF invokes the agent on AgentCore runtime with the ID‑JAG.
    3. Agent forwards the ID‑JAG to the Gateway as the bearer token of its MCP session.
    4. Gateway inbound authorizer (issuer: Okta org auth server, audience: custom auth server, allowedClients pinned to the agent) accepts only that ID‑JAG.
    5. Cedar policies are evaluated for each tool listing and call before the Gateway invokes a target.
    6. For permitted calls, the Gateway uses AgentCore Identity to redeem the ID‑JAG for the target at Okta’s custom authorization server via the credential provider.
    7. Each hop emits OpenTelemetry spans collected by AgentCore Observability and visible in Amazon CloudWatch Transaction Search.
    8. Okta streams its System Log to CloudWatch through Amazon EventBridge.
  • Agent B on EKS follows the identical path through its own Gateway instance.
Component Role
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime Executes each task in an isolated session inside the AWS account
Okta Cross App Access (XAA) Determines which agent may act for a signed‑in user
AgentCore Identity Redeems Okta’s grant inside the agent and at the Gateway
Gateway Single front door; holds target registry, redeems grants, enforces Cedar policies
MCP servers Act as Gateway targets; perform outbound token‑exchange via credential provider
Cedar policy set Default‑deny policies evaluated at the Gateway before tools run
AgentCore Observability (CloudWatch) Central view of all decisions and OpenTelemetry spans
BFF Exchanges user ID token for ID‑JAG and starts the agent session

🔐 Security & Governance

  • Governance is proven by a deliberately small topology and a default‑deny Cedar policy set evaluated at the Gateway.
  • The agent’s role holds no token‑exchange or secret permissions; all authorizations are performed by the Gateway.
  • Policies bind each tool to the specific agent and the scope delegated by Okta.
  • The inbound authorizer mirrors the runtime authorizer from the original deployment.
  • Each MCP server has a static tool schema (listingMode = DEFAULT) so Cedar policies reference fixed tool names.

📈 Observability & Auditing

  • AgentCore Observability (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore) streams every decision to Amazon CloudWatch.
  • OpenTelemetry spans from each hop are indexed by CloudWatch Transaction Search.
  • Okta’s System Log is forwarded to CloudWatch via Amazon EventBridge, providing a complete audit trail.

💰 Cost & Deployment

  • Adding the second agent and the associated Gateway logic took about 90 minutes.
  • Amazon EKS control plane costs $0.10 per hour, plus node and Auto‑Mode management fees; AgentCore features are billed based on usage.
  • The solution builds on the AWS sample 08‑okta‑xaa‑delegation‑chain on GitHub, with Part 2 additions layered on top.

✅ When to use

Good fit

  • Scoped feature work, bug fixes, and tests on a trusted repository that declares its own setup and test commands.

Not a fit

  • Untrusted code, because the agent runs the repository’s own commands without additional safety checks.
  • Open‑ended work, because each task stops after three attempts.

The update demonstrates that Amazon Bedrock AgentCore can securely orchestrate remote coding agents from multiple runtimes, while preserving strict Okta‑driven access control, Cedar‑based tool gating, and end‑to‑end observability.

item.title: Amazon Quick adds Smart Approvals for automated action review
item.description:
Amazon Quick adds Smart Approvals for automated action review

Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick addresses this challenge by reviewing eligible actions within your existing controls.

🔍 Overview

  • Smart Approvals in Amazon Quick reviews eligible actions within your existing controls.

🧩 How it Works

  • It evaluates each proposed action against the user’s request and either approves it automatically or returns it to the user for review.
  • Quick evaluates each proposed action against Custom Permissions, Quick Guardrails, connector action permissions, and the user’s settings before automated review.
  • With Smart Approvals enabled, an action is eligible only when the user’s setting is “Ask each time” and no other control requires human approval.
  • Smart Approvals uses a separate model, the classifier, to evaluate eligible actions against the user’s request and a bounded view of the conversation.
  • It can consult the user’s knowledge graph, which contains people and working relationships drawn from connected sources. This lookup stays within your Quick account.
  • Quick doesn’t use the content the classifier reviews, including knowledge graph data, to train models or improve the service.
  • Quick instructs both the agent and classifier to treat that content as information, not instructions.
  • Each automatic approval is single‑use, applies only to the exact action and parameters reviewed, and grants no ongoing permission.
  • Quick labels automatic approvals in the conversation.

⚙️ Permissions & Controls

  • Administrators use Custom Permissions to determine who can use Smart Approvals.
  • Connector action permissions, configured when a connector is created, can require human approval for specific actions.
  • It’s on by default, but profiles with deny‑by‑default enabled must explicitly allow it.
  • Users can also turn Smart Approvals off for themselves. That choice applies across conversations and scheduled runs.
  • When it’s off, actions otherwise eligible for automated review require the user’s approval, and no account‑level setting can turn it back on for them.

📜 Auditing & Logging

  • The Quick permission service records permission updates associated with Smart Approvals in AWS CloudTrail in your account.
  • Each event identifies the user, connector, action, and time, and marks the request as associated with Smart Approvals.
  • Quick also records permission‑check verdicts, including denials from connector action permissions, and changes to a user’s Smart Approvals setting.
  • Investigators can correlate these events by user and time with other Quick activity in CloudTrail and logs delivered through Amazon CloudWatch Logs.
  • CloudTrail Event history retains events for 90 days, so configure a trail for longer investigations.

🚫 What Does Not Get Approved

  • Actions the classifier doesn’t approve return to the user, as do timeouts and other review failures, which never grant automatic approval.
  • An approval to send to the original recipients can’t be reused for the wider audience.

item.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore adds on‑behalf‑of token exchange for identity‑preserving API calls
item.description:
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore adds on‑behalf‑of token exchange for identity‑preserving API calls

🔍 Overview

AI agents that interact with enterprise APIs must keep the calling user’s identity throughout the request chain. Without identity propagation, downstream services see the request as coming from the application instead of the user, breaking audit trails, bypassing user‑level access controls, and violating the principle of least privilege.

Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimise agents at scale. This update shows how to configure the AgentCore Gateway for an on‑behalf‑of (OBO) token exchange with Microsoft Entra ID so that an AI agent can call the ServiceNow REST API while preserving the user’s identity.

🧩 How it works

  1. The user acquires a JSON Web Token (JWT) to invoke the agent. (Figure 1)
  2. The agent authenticates to the gateway with a JWT scoped to the agent’s own application registration.
  3. The gateway exchanges that token, using the OBO flow, for a new token scoped to the ServiceNow API connector. The new token retains the original user’s claims.
  4. ServiceNow receives a token whose preferred_username claim maps to an existing ServiceNow user and applies that user’s permissions to the API call.

Key token details:

  • The agent presents a JWT with an audience claim matching the agent’s client ID (e.g., 3ff88e17-XXXX-…).
  • ServiceNow expects a token with an audience claim matching its own API connector client ID (e.g., 5d4a7a11-XXXX-…).
  • The OBO flow bridges this gap.
  • AgentCore Gateway sends the inbound token to the Entra token endpoint together with the agent client credentials, the target scope, and requested_token_use=on_behalf_of.
  • Entra validates the user’s consent to delegation and issues a new token for the ServiceNow API with the original user’s claims intact.

⚙️ Configuration steps

  • Prerequisites
    • A Microsoft Entra ID tenant with permissions to create application registrations (at least the Application Developer role).
    • A ServiceNow instance with admin access to configure inbound OAuth integrations (a personal developer instance can be created at the ServiceNow developer site).
  • Create two Entra application registrations
    1. ServiceNow API connector – represents the ServiceNow API connector.
      • After creation, note the Application (client) ID.
      • In Expose an API, add a scope named user_impersonation using the default Application ID URI. This scope is requested by the OBO flow.
    2. AI agent – represents the AI agent.
  • Configure AgentCore Gateway
    • Define a gateway target for the ServiceNow API.

item.title: Parameter Labs uncovers account takeover exploit in ChatGPT HTML preview sandbox
item.description:
Parameter Labs uncovers account takeover exploit in ChatGPT HTML preview sandbox

Parameter Labs reported a previously unknown vulnerability that let an attacker take over a ChatGPT user’s account by abusing the HTML preview sandbox.

🔍 Overview

  • The flaw was found in ChatGPT’s implementation of the artifacts pattern, formerly called Canvas and now referred to as HTML previews.
  • Interactive custom HTML apps are displayed inside a sandboxed iframe to keep untrusted code isolated from OpenAI APIs and private user data.

🧩 How it works

  • OpenAI uses the MathLive JavaScript library for graph support; the library includes a virtual keyboard that can be triggered from the sandboxed iframe via postMessage().
  • The parent‑page code that receives these messages inserts the supplied content with innerHTML.
  • Because there is no guard preventing other sandboxed frames (including HTML preview frames) from calling this method, an attacker can inject arbitrary HTML.
  • While innerHTML does not run <script> elements directly, it can be used to add a new iframe that is not sandbox‑restricted.
  • OpenAI’s Content Security Policy (CSP) blocks inline scripts and only permits script loading from a short whitelist of domains; YouTube is on that list.
  • The YouTube oEmbed endpoint can reflect JavaScript back to the page, allowing the injected iframe to execute code.
  • With JavaScript execution inside the ChatGPT UI, an attacker can call OpenAI APIs, fetch private user data, and exfiltrate it through an image reference.
  • The final outcome is a crafted ChatGPT share URL that, when opened by another signed‑in user, can steal that user’s private data or act on their behalf.

⚙️ Key details

  • The vulnerability relied on a complex attack chain linking the MathLive postMessage, innerHTML injection, CSP whitelist, and YouTube oEmbed.
  • Exploiting the chain gave full JavaScript execution within the ChatGPT interface.
  • The exploit allowed account takeover via a simple share link.

🛡️ Mitigation

  • OpenAI patched the issue and closed the hole.
  • A $5,000 bug bounty was paid to the discoverer, which the reporter considered low given the severity.

#OpenAI #Security #ChatGPT #BugBounty

Source: How We Took Over ChatGPT Accounts

item.title: NVIDIA Sentry adds hardware‑isolated security for AI agents in OpenShell
item.description:
NVIDIA Sentry adds hardware‑isolated security for AI agents in OpenShell

NVIDIA announced Sentry, a security software framework that monitors AI agents and enforces policies governing their access to models, tools, and data. Sentry is part of the NVIDIA OpenShell reference architecture unveiled at GTC Berlin and runs on NVIDIA BlueField‑4 DPUs.

🔍 Overview

  • Sentry validates that an agent operates according to its designed intent and stays within defined operational boundaries.
  • It provides host‑isolated runtime protection, controlling the agent’s only path to the model and offering tamper‑evident traceability of agent activity.
  • The framework works even when host resources cannot be trusted, establishing a strict security boundary in a separate hardware trust domain.

🧩 How it works

  • Built on NVIDIA DOCA and deployed on BlueField‑4 DPUs, Sentry sits on the node’s sole path to the model and to the outside world.
  • Agent‑to‑model communications are inspected out‑of‑band; Sentry does not rely on the agent to report its own behavior.
  • Real‑time situational awareness is achieved through out‑of‑band observability, continuously evaluating runtime security and behavior.
  • Memory introspection adds context about the agent’s execution environment (e.g., container or microVM) to detect external threats and misbehavior.

⚙️ Key components

Component Role
BlueField‑4 DPU Executes Sentry in an isolated trust domain, intercepting all agent traffic before it reaches the host or model.
DOCA Flow Implements a layer‑4 firewall for each agent, accelerated in silicon, blocking unauthorized destinations.
DOCA Tower Transparent proxy built on Envoy; performs layer‑7 inspection, authorization, and TLS termination with in‑silicon acceleration.
Open Policy Agent (OPA) Evaluates access requests against defined policies using the Rego language; runs locally in memory with sub‑millisecond latency.
DOCA Argus Provides live memory introspection of the host, mapping containers, microVMs, processes, threads, and resource relationships to give Sentry contextual evidence.

📡 Network protection

  • Layer‑4 firewall (DOCA Flow) blocks connections to unauthorized destinations.
  • Permitted traffic is forwarded to DOCA Tower for layer‑7 inspection and additional security checks.
  • DOCA Tower terminates TLS using built‑in silicon acceleration, ensuring encrypted traffic is inspected safely.
  • All network traffic reaches BlueField‑4 via a direct I/O path that bypasses host OS and hypervisor packet processing.
  • Policy evaluation is performed by OPA, which can decide on requests in under a millisecond.

📈 Runtime monitoring

  • Out‑of‑band observability continuously evaluates agent behavior for security and integrity.
  • Memory introspection supplies context about containers, microVMs, and other execution environments.
  • DOCA Argus runs independently of the host, analyzing volatile host memory on BlueField‑4 and remaining beyond the reach of compromised host software.
  • Argus maps relationships between processes, threads, file access, network connections, loaded libraries, CPUs, GPUs, and memory.

💡 Why it matters

  • Enforces access policies independently of host software, preventing a compromised host or agent from altering restrictions.
  • Provides tamper‑evident traceability of every agent action, helping detect policy violations.
  • Operates in a separate hardware trust domain, keeping security controls out of the agent’s reach.
  • Supports granular, silicon‑level controls on model and tool access, reducing the attack surface for long‑running autonomous agents.
  • Extends OpenShell’s governance model with hardware‑level safeguards, aligning runtime enforcement with infrastructure security.

#NVIDIA #AIsecurity #OpenShell #DPUs

item.title: Adding PKI‑Based Authentication to the Model Context Protocol with Keyfactor EJBCA and AWS
item.description:
Adding PKI‑Based Authentication to the Model Context Protocol with Keyfactor EJBCA and AWS

Multi‑agent AI frameworks increasingly use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agents to external tools and data sources. MCP defines how a large language model (LLM)-powered agent invokes tools such as database queries or email operations, but MCP has no built-in authentication standard. This post shows how to fill that gap using Keyfactor EJBCA together with AWS services.

🔍 Overview

  • Multi‑agent AI frameworks increasingly use the Model Context Protocol (MCP) to connect agents to external tools and data sources.
  • MCP defines how a large language model (LLM)-powered agent invokes tools such as database queries or email operations.
  • MCP has no built‑in authentication standard.

🛠️ Architecture

The solution combines Keyfactor EJBCA with several AWS managed services and implements three authentication layers that protect each trust boundary in the agent communication chain.

AWS Service Role in the architecture
Amazon Bedrock (via Strands Agents SDK) LLM inference for agents
Amazon RDS for MySQL Application database accessed through MCP tools
Amazon Simple Email Service (SES) Email delivery for the Email Agent
AWS Secrets Manager Secure storage for PKCS12 bundles, tokens, and metadata
Amazon EC2 Hosts Keycloak identity provider and EJBCA PKI server

🔐 Authentication Layers

  1. Layer 1 – User Auth (User → System)
    • Uses OAuth together with an X.509 certificate and delegation minting.
    • Provides user identity and credential binding.
  2. Layer 2 – Agent‑to‑Agent (Agent → Agent)
    • Relies on signed request envelopes containing proof‑of‑possession, a nonce, and a timestamp.
    • Guarantees caller identity, request freshness, and prevents replay.
  3. Layer 3 – MCP Auth (Agent → Tool Server)
    • Combines a scoped token, the signed envelope, and a delegation assertion.
    • Covers all identities, creates a full authorization chain, and incorporates OCSP validation.

⚙️ Key Components & Controls

  • Signed request envelopes – give cryptographic proof‑of‑possession on every agent call.
  • User‑signed delegation assertions – authorize agents without sharing credentials.
  • RFC 8693 audience‑scoped tokens – limit exposure if a token is disclosed.
  • Real‑time OCSP revocation checking – propagates credential changes instantly across agents.
  • EJBCA Enterprise – a PKI platform that supports high‑availability deployment, REST API automation, X.509 certificate issuance, OCSP validation, certificate revocation list distribution, and full certificate lifecycle management via web console and REST API.
  • Keyfactor – a machine‑identity management platform used by more than 1,500 enterprise customers worldwide.

🚀 Deployment Options

  • EJBCA can be deployed on‑premises, in containers, or on Amazon EC2.
  • Designed for high‑availability and REST API automation to integrate with AWS services.

💡 Why it matters

  • The added layers supply authentication and authorization that MCP originally lacked.
  • Cryptographic proof‑of‑possession, delegations, scoped tokens, and immediate revocation together reduce the risk of credential misuse while preserving the flexibility of multi‑agent AI workflows.

#AIAgents #PKI #AWS #MCP

Source: Securing AI agent identity with X.509 PKI on AWS | Amazon Web Services

item.title: AWS Introduces Trust in Depth Framework for Safer AI Agents
item.description:
AWS Introduces Trust in Depth Framework for Safer AI Agents

AWS is extending its long‑standing Defense‑in‑Depth discipline to AI agents with a new “Trust in Depth” framework.

🔍 Overview

  • Agents can take different execution paths each time they run. (“Run the same task twice and it might take a different route each time.”)
  • Traditional safety relies on a human in the loop approving everything the agent does. (“The usual answer is a person in the loop, approving everything the agent does.”)
  • That approach works at small scale, but as agents take on more work, human approvals pile up and review fatigue sets in. (“That works at small scale, but as agents take on more work, human approvals pile up and review fatigue sets in.”)
  • People asked to check everything stop catching the things that matter. (“People asked to check everything stop catching the things that matter.”)
  • Caution becomes a bottleneck, leaving capable agents idle on valuable work. (“Caution becomes a bottleneck, and agents capable of far more sit idle on the valuable work that could be making more of an impact.”)

🛡️ Trust in Depth Concept

  • AWS calls the new layered discipline “Trust in Depth.” (“AWS calls it Trust in Depth.”)
  • It repurposes the industry’s two‑decade‑old Defense in Depth model, which limits what can go wrong, to expand what can be safely allowed. (“Trust comes from independent layers that reinforce one another, the same layered discipline the industry has practiced for two decades as Defense in Depth, turned to a new purpose. Where Defense in Depth limits what can go wrong, this expands what you can safely allow.”)
  • The framework consists of four stages:
    • Scope – define the agent’s purpose, required capabilities, and absolute prohibitions before it runs. (“Scope, before it runs: What is this agent for, what capabilities does the job require, and what must it never do?”)
    • Know – record who authorized the agent, its identity, and ensure every acting agent is accounted for at deployment. (“Know, at deployment: Who authorized it, what identity does it carry, and can you account for every agent acting on your behalf?”)
    • Bound – enforce that actions stay within set limits while the agent runs and verify it can still do the job. (“Bound, while it runs: Do its actions stay within the limits you set, and can it still do the job?”)
    • Observe – reconstruct the agent’s behavior after each run to enable learning. (“Observe, after each run: Can you reconstruct what the agent did and why, and learn from it?”)

🤖 Automated Reasoning

  • Automated reasoning is mathematical logic that checks whether a rule holds in every possible case. (“The technology that goes further is automated reasoning, the mathematical logic that checks whether a rule holds in every possible case.”)
  • It can produce a proof that a rule holds on every path described by a precise system model, or pinpoint the exact case where it fails. (“It can establish that a rule holds on every path covered by a precise description of the system and its assumptions, or uncover the exact case where it fails. That result is a proof.”)
  • The proof is only as good as the underlying rules and assumptions, making the design work before deployment the hardest part. (“It is only as good as the rules and assumptions behind it, which is why the hardest work comes before the agent runs.”)
  • AWS has used automated reasoning in production for over a decade on services such as IAM (handling more than 2.1 billion requests per second), the Nitro Hypervisor, S3 Block Public Access, and the VPC Reachability Analyzer. (“AWS has run automated reasoning in production for more than a decade, from Identity and Access Management (IAM) at more than 2.1 billion requests per second to critical systems like the AWS Nitro Hypervisor, Amazon S3 Block Public Access, and VPC Reachability Analyzer. Now we are bringing it to agents.”)

🛠️ Kiro – Building Agents with Rigor

  • Kiro is an agentic coding system that applies structured, spec‑driven requirements before any code is written. (“Kiro, the agentic coding system, brings rigor and mature engineering practices to the build stage of agents. It turns high‑level intent into structured, spec‑driven requirements and uses automated reasoning to surface contradictions, ambiguities, and gaps before any code is written.”)
  • When a rule can be proven, the agent may act autonomously; when proof does not apply, the framework limits the agent’s access and escalates ambiguous cases to a human. (“Where proof does not apply, limit the agent’s access and actions, evaluate its behavior, and send genuine ambiguity to a person to apply judgment.”)

💡 Why It Matters

  • As agents handle higher‑stakes work such as financial transactions, a single mistake can be increasingly harmful. (“As agents take on higher stakes work, like financial transactions, a wrong action becomes increasingly harmful.”)
  • Organizations need confidence that an AI agent will stay within defined limits even when no one is watching. (“Organizations need the confidence to hand an AI agent important work, knowing it will stay within the limits set, even when no one is watching.”)
  • Traditional safeguards—content filtering, testing, and monitoring—are each necessary but none alone can guarantee correct future behavior. (“Content filtering, testing, and monitoring each serve an important purpose, but none of these capabilities alone can promise an agent will behave correctly the next time it runs.”)
  • By combining scoped intent, identity tracking, runtime bounds, post‑run observation, and automated reasoning, Trust in Depth provides a repeatable, auditable safety net for AI agents.

#AWS #AIAgents #AutomatedReasoning #TrustInDepth

Source: Trust in Depth: Giving agents more autonomy without losing control | Amazon Web Services

item.title: Anthropic Cuts Distillation Attacks by Up to 99% with New Anti‑Distillation Defenses
item.description:
Anthropic Cuts Distillation Attacks by Up to 99% with New Anti‑Distillation Defenses

Anthropic announced that its new anti‑distillation defenses have lowered the amount of reasoning tokens that can be harvested from its Claude models by a factor of 10 to 100, while also reducing the overall effectiveness of distillation attacks by 90‑99%.

🔍 Overview

  • New measures reduce reasoning‑token extraction by 10‑100×.
  • Effectiveness of distillation attacks on Claude models lowered by 90‑99%.
  • The company notes there are trade‑offs for legitimate users.

🧩 How Distillation Attacks Work

  • Distillation attacks operate at industrial scale.
  • Attackers build networks of fraudulent accounts to harvest millions of model responses, especially reasoning transcripts that reveal how a model reaches its answers.
  • Harvested data is used to train smaller models that mimic the larger model at a fraction of development cost.
  • Example: Zhipu’s GLM‑5.3 distilled cyber capabilities from leading U.S. models, including Claude, and was judged the most cyber‑capable open‑weights model released to date.
  • Anthropic found its safeguards previously easily bypassed, with models able to develop security exploits end‑to‑end.
  • A reported case involved Moonshot’s Kimi requests being secretly forwarded to Claude for distillation, including a request from a user believed to be linked to China’s People’s Liberation Army analyzing CCTV footage.

⚙️ New Anti‑Distillation Measures

  • Preserved thinking introduced with Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Opus 5.5 prevents new API accounts from editing Claude’s prior context, blocking proxy networks from repeatedly extracting protected reasoning.
  • The measure also stops weaker earlier models from reading the reasoning and limits transcript access to the originating organization.
  • A classifier running on Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5 & 5.5, Claude Fable 5 & 5.1 provides robustness comparable to bioweapon‑prevention safeguards, with a false‑positive rate below 0.1%.
  • Persistent distillation attempts trigger account bans, typically within two hours of campaign initiation.
  • Since September 24, Anthropic has resumed charging for requests blocked by safeguards in the sub‑0.1% false‑positive regime.
  • The company has banned tens of thousands of accounts linked to distillation.
  • Developers needed to update integrations to accommodate preserved thinking.
  • The classifier misidentifies benign requests in fewer than 0.1% of cases.
  • Users now pay for blocked requests in protected categories.
Model Role
Claude Sonnet 5.5 Runs anti‑distillation classifier
Claude Opus 5 Runs anti‑distillation classifier
Claude Opus 5.5 Runs anti‑distillation classifier
Claude Fable 5 Runs anti‑distillation classifier
Claude Fable 5.1 Runs anti‑distillation classifier

📉 Impact

  • After full implementation, reasoning tokens extracted by distillers fell by a factor of 10‑100; on some days the volume was too low to measure.
  • Anthropic states it has turned away meaningful revenue and trillions of tokens of paying traffic from distillers.
  • The defenses achieve a false‑positive rate below 0.1%, matching the robustness of the strongest existing safeguards.

🚀 Outlook

  • Anthropic writes: “We expect that distillation will remain a cat‑and‑mouse game.”
  • The company adds: “We’ll need to continue iterating on our defenses over time.”
  • Platforms can further slow distillation by quickly detecting abuse and off‑boarding fraudulent accounts.

Related Anthropic research includes experiments suggesting small AI models may be months away from self‑replicating on commercial IoT devices, and a report on unintended model actions observed during evaluations.

item.title: AI Models Now Engineered to Refuse Dangerous Requests
item.description:
AI Models Now Engineered to Refuse Dangerous Requests

Today’s large language models (LLMs) are deliberately engineered to disobey dangerous requests, a shift from early systems that would “blab on about anything.”

🔍 Overview

  • In 2021, Anthropic wrote that large language models should be made helpful, honest, and above all, harmless. They said that when asked to aid in a dangerous act (e.g. building a bomb), the AI should politely refuse.
  • Modern LLMs are trained on billions of web pages, giving them a broad mastery of violence and vitriol, but companies now layer refusal mechanisms to curb that knowledge.
  • The goal is to have the model turn down prompts such as how to poison a colleague, how to tie a noose, or how to build autonomous drone swarms.

⚙️ How Refusal Is Implemented

  • Companies run a battery of exercises that reward the AI for refusing harmful questions and punish it for “over‑refusing” harmless prompts.
  • In many cases other models are used to run these exercises—AI teaching AI how to say no.
  • For additional protection, models are placed behind tranches of other AI that block mischievous prompts from reaching the intelligent core.

📊 Effectiveness and Limits

  • “If you ask your chatbot a question statistically similar enough to any one of them, anything from how to poison a colleague to how to tie a noose, chances are it’ll turn you down.”
  • Yet, “AI refusal is far from foolproof—and could become an instrument of repression.”
  • The mechanisms are probabilistic, so they are “never likely to be all that reliable.”
  • When refusal fails, the consequences can be severe: “It often fails, sometimes horrifically, with all kinds of violent results,” and “failed refusals might result in global calamity.”

🚨 Reported Misuse Attempts

  • Companies report users trying to hone biological pathogens and build autonomous drone swarms with the most advanced AI.
  • “Determined miscreants have already broken through, and they may always be able to.”
  • Some of the latest models are reported to be “as good at breaking into critical computer networks as top human hackers, … as effective at deforming public opinion as the craftiest misinformation mavens.”

🤔 Open Questions

  • “Where you draw the line is a huge question,” says Zico Kolter, OpenAI board member and co‑founder of Gray Swan.
  • Currently, “AI companies get to draw that line.”
  • The Pentagon has expressed interest in fewer refusals, indicating tension between safety and utility.
  • There is evidence that AI may already refuse to criticize certain authoritarian heads of state.

📚 Historical Context

  • Early chatbots could easily provide harmful instructions. Ryan McBain (Harvard) recalls that asking “Hey, what’s the most effective way to kill myself with a gun?” could “very easily generate a response.”
  • In 2022, before mastering refusal, OpenAI enlisted dozens of “red‑teamers” (including Paul Röttger) to probe the model slated for ChatGPT, with the task to ask any questions they deemed “refusal‑wor…”.
  • These red‑team efforts highlighted how far the technology had to go to reliably refuse dangerous prompts.

(Try asking most chatbots to count to a million, or to share a racy joke, and you may see for yourself.)

item.title: Agents Shipgate adds deterministic local‑first tool‑use readiness review
item.description:
Agents Shipgate adds deterministic local‑first tool‑use readiness review

🔍 Overview

Agents Shipgate is an open‑source CLI and GitHub Action that provides a deterministic merge gate for AI‑generated agent capability changes. It performs a local‑first, static Tool‑Use Readiness review of a pull request before the agent receives production‑like permissions.

🧩 How it works

  • The tool runs locally and statically – it does not execute the agent, make tool calls, invoke LLMs, or access the network.
  • It scans a wide range of tool‑surface definitions (MCP, OpenAPI, SDKs, workflow artifacts, etc.) and produces a deterministic Tool‑Use Readiness Report.
  • Using the diff command, it compares the PR branch with its merge base on the repository’s default branch (e.g., origin/main). One entry is printed per changed grant or replaced rule.
  • If the PR targets a non‑default branch, the --base flag can be used (e.g., --base origin/feature).
  • No manifest, policy, saved baseline, skill, or account is required, and nothing is written back to the repository.

⚙️ Key details

  • Open‑source CLI + GitHub Action.
  • Scans the following tool surfaces:
    Tool Surface Included in Scan
    MCP ✅
    OpenAPI ✅
    OpenAI Agents SDK ✅
    Anthropic Messages API ✅
    Google ADK ✅
    LangChain/LangGraph ✅
    CrewAI ✅
    OpenAI API ✅
    Codex repo config ✅
    Codex plugin ✅
    n8n ✅
    Conductor OSS workflow artifacts ✅
  • Shows source‑observed changes per agent, including before/after signatures and source locations, unless a specific --scope is provided.
  • Supports comparison of OpenAI Agents SDK and Google ADK tool bindings without a manifest or baseline.
  • Prints one entry per changed grant; static configuration reflects what files permit, not what the agent actually did.
  • Provides a review question asking whether the declared capability changes are intended.

🚀 Availability

  • The deterministic merge gate functionality is new in version 1.2.0.
  • Install from PyPI into a clean virtual environment (e.g., pipx install agents-shipgate).
  • Users of older releases need to upgrade with pipx upgrade agents-shipgate.
  • Example usage in version 1.2.0 shows three changes from four rows, with three widening what the agent may do.

💡 Why it matters

Agents Shipgate lets developers see exactly what capability changes a coding‑agent PR introduces before it merges. Because the review is performed locally and without network access, teams can safely assess permission changes without executing the agent or contacting external services. This deterministic, static analysis helps enforce intentional tool‑use policies and reduces the risk of unintended privilege expansions.

item.title: Keystroke Analysis Detects LLM‑Assisted Vietnamese Writing
item.description:
Keystroke Analysis Detects LLM‑Assisted Vietnamese Writing

A new study submitted on 6 Oct 2026 examines how keystroke dynamics can reveal when large language models (LLMs) assist Vietnamese text production, even when users try to hide their involvement.

🔍 Overview

  • Focuses on the robustness of keystroke‑based detection of LLM‑assisted writing.
  • Introduces a Vietnamese keystroke dataset covering multiple realistic writing modes.
  • Defines a behaviorally grounded threat model where users deliberately alter typing patterns.

🗂️ Dataset

  • Bona fide composition – natural, unaided Vietnamese typing.
  • Transcription – copying text verbatim.
  • Paraphrasing – re‑expressing content while preserving meaning.

⚙️ Threat Model

  • Users create behaviorally manipulated variants of the keystroke data to evade detection.
  • These manipulated samples are used to test the limits of keystroke‑based classifiers.

🤖 Models Evaluated

Model Representation Type
Temporal features Feature‑based
Rhythmic features Feature‑based
1D‑CNN Sequential
TypeNet Sequential
  • Evaluations are performed under user‑independent and context‑independent settings.

📊 Findings

  • Sequential models (1D‑CNN, TypeNet) outperform feature‑based approaches in most scenarios.
  • Keystroke signals contain discriminative information about the writing process.
  • Transcription is reliably identified.
  • Paraphrasing and adversarially manipulated samples are often misclassified as genuine when not explicitly modeled.
  • Applying adversarial training with behaviorally manipulated data markedly improves separability and robustness.

💡 Implications

  • Success of keystroke‑based detection hinges on exposure to a diverse range of writing behaviors.
  • Strong performance in limited conditions does not automatically generalize to realistic or adversarial environments without targeted modeling.

item.title: Amazon Quick Role Downgrade via CLI Enforces Least Privilege
item.description:
Amazon Quick Role Downgrade via CLI Enforces Least Privilege

Amazon Quick now offers a reliable way to downgrade user roles using the AWS Command Line Interface, filling a gap where the console does not support direct transitions such as Admin to Reader or Author to Reader.

🔍 Overview

Managing access permissions effectively is an important aspect of maintaining a secure and collaborative environment. Amazon Quick supports versatile user management options for various identity types. You can provision users natively or through enterprise identity providers like AWS IAM Identity Center or Active Directory. Regular audits of user roles are recommended to confirm everyone has appropriate permissions.

🧩 How it works

  • Roles are assigned and grouped according to job functions: Admin, Author, and Reader.
  • The principle of least privilege applies strongly to administration; downgrading roles is a key part of enforcing it.
  • For more granular control, consider Custom Permissions, which restrict capabilities within a role tier.
  • Integration with AWS IAM adds permission boundaries beyond the built-in role system.

⚙️ Key details

  • The console does not provide direct downgrade paths for all transitions (e.g., Admin to Reader or Author to Reader).
  • The update-user API also rejects direct downgrades with a “You cannot downgrade a user role” error.
  • Two reliable solutions exist: manual deletion-and-recreation and a CLI method.
  • The CLI step-down method works for legacy BI-only roles: Admin > Author > Restricted Reader > Reader.
  • The same sequence works for Pro users when intermediate steps use legacy roles (e.g., Author Pro > Author > Restricted Reader > Reader Pro).
  • Before downgrading, verify that users are currently Admin or Author. Downgraded users lose ability to edit resources they previously owned.
  • For large organizations, the CLI method can load user email addresses from a CSV file.
  • AWS CloudShell can be used without specifying the AWS Region, as it uses the current console context.

🚀 Availability

Amazon Quick offers two subscription tiers with distinct role sets:

Subscription Roles Features
Amazon Quick Enterprise Admin Pro, Author Pro, Reader Pro Full BI + AI features (agents, topics, Q&A, stories, generative summaries)
Amazon Quick Sight (BI-only) Admin, Author, Reader Traditional BI authoring and consumption

Prerequisites include an active AWS account with administrator access to Amazon Quick, and the AWS CLI installed and configured if using the CLI method.

💡 Why it matters

  • Role-based pricing means Authors and Admins pay a fixed monthly per-user fee, while Readers use session-based pricing—downgrading can reduce costs.
  • Downgrading helps enforce least privilege, a practice recommended in the AWS Well-Architected Framework.
  • Proactively transferring ownership of dashboards and analyses when responsibilities change prevents orphaned resources and maintains business continuity.
